title: Invert a Signed 32-Bit Integer

content.problemStatement:
You receive a signed 32-bit integer x, reverse its decimal digits while preserving its sign. Omit leading zeroes from the reversed representation.

The task is to output 0 if the reversed value is outside the signed 32-bit range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].
constraints: Do not use 64-bit integer arithmetic to compute the reversed value; detect overflow using 32-bit checks.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Reversing the decimal digits 1, 2, and 3 produces 321, which remains within the signed 32-bit range.
Reverse the magnitude 123 to obtain 321, then preserve the negative sign. The result is -321.
Reversing 120 gives 021; leading zeroes are omitted in an integer value, leaving 21.

notes: All hidden test cases are concrete and use the documented JSON argument format.

solution.approach: Iteratively extract digits from the input using pop = x % 10 and x = x / 10 (truncating toward zero). Before each multiply/add step check 32-bit overflow using INT_MAX/INT_MIN thresholds. Do not convert the input to a positive value (avoid abs(INT_MIN) or x * -1).

hints: If numRows is 1 or numRows >= len(s), return s immediately to avoid extra work.
Simulate the zigzag by keeping an array of row buffers and a direction flag (down/up) that flips at the top and bottom rows.
Alternatively compute positions using cycle = 2 * numRows - 2 and append characters for each row using arithmetic to avoid per-character direction logic.
followUps: Return the mapping from each output character back to its original index (useful for index-tracking or highlighting).
Adapt the algorithm to work on a character stream (infinite or very large input) so you never store the entire string in memory.
Generalize the pattern to arbitrary row traversal orders (e.g., custom down/up lengths or repeating patterns) and compute positions efficiently.
learningObjectives: Model a simple state machine (row index + direction) to transform sequences.
Apply modular arithmetic and cycle reasoning to compute repeated patterns.
Handle edge cases in string algorithms (short strings, single row, trailing/leading characters).
Compare time/space trade-offs between simulation and index-computation approaches.
